10868-clerambault-the-story-of-an-indepe:
Romain Rolland's Clerambault, translated by Katherine Miller in 1921, tells of an independent spirit during the First World War. Rolland warns readers that the book is not a novel, nor an autobiography: it is the confession of a free spirit, telling its mistakes, sufferings, and struggles from inside the tempest. He lent his hero some ideas, but the man's character and life are his own.

Clerambault wanders an inward labyrinth, uncertain and sensitive, yet sincere and ardent for truth. Some chapters recall the French moralists and the stoical essays of the sixteenth century. Readers get a searching portrait of conscience under wartime passion, by a Nobel laureate.
12049-legal-status-of-women-in-iowa:
Jennie L. Wilson, LL.B., member of the Polk County Bar, compiled Legal Status of Women in Iowa, published in Des Moines by the Iowa Printing Company in 1894. Her preface states the book's purpose: to present to the women of Iowa, in brief and concise form, the laws on subjects in which they are most deeply interested. About which there is a strong and growing demand for certain and accurate information.

Wilson covers property, marriage, divorce, guardianship, and other topics where law touched women's daily lives, at a time when married women's rights were still being reformed state by state. The compilation served lawyers, clubwomen, and ordinary readers who needed to know, in plain form, what Iowa law actually said.
1452-native-life-in-south-africa-before-:
Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje, a South African writer and activist, writes of native life in South Africa before and since the European war and the Boer rebellion. Plaatje, a founder of the African National Congress, speaks from inside. Plaatje wrote the book in 1916, protesting the Natives Land Act of 1913.

He describes land laws, dispossession, and daily hardship under the Natives Land Act, with testimony and argument. The book remains a landmark of South African protest writing, and a firsthand record of injustice. His testimony, gathered from chiefs and farmers, gave the protest its human face.
17616-little-sky-high-or-the-surprising-:
Hezekiah Butterworth, author of In the Days of Jefferson and Little Arthur's History of Rome, wrote this children's story of Little Sky-High and the surprising doings of Washee-Washee-Wang. The book belongs to the Nine to Twelve series from Thomas Y. Crowell and Company of New York, alongside stories by Kate Gannett Wells and Harriet Prescott Spofford. A picture shows a great mouth opening, with smoke seeming to issue from it.

Readers get a fanciful tale for children of nine to twelve, full of surprise and humour in Butterworth's kindly manner. The book suits young readers who enjoy tall tales and exotic names. Its series setting marks it as part of a graded children's library.
18174-some-winter-days-in-iowa:
Frederick John Lazell published this 1907 nature book from Cedar Rapids, Iowa. Lazell argues that people turn to nature for relief from toil and strife, and that the wish to leave city streets for woodland, field, and stream was growing in his day. Cities were buying parks, and states and the nation were setting aside wild tracts for the public.

His first essay, The Woodlands in January, opens that theme in winter dress. Later pages follow Iowa fields and woods through the cold months, with birds, tracks, and the quiet of snow. Readers get a gentle Iowa natural history, written for walkers who want to see their own country with fresh eyes in the hardest season.
18227-some-spring-days-in-iowa:
Frederick John Lazell wrote Some Spring Days in Iowa, printed in Cedar Rapids in 1908 by the Torch Press. Lazell, who signs his preface from Cedar Rapids on December 1, 1908, gives spring in the Iowa river country with a naturalist's eye.

April brings buds and bird songs, with a strong southeast wind driving whitecaps up the river. A song sparrow sings its recitative on a canyon ledge, and the writer dreams of Danton, Tennyson, and Canute. Lazell writes with quiet, lyrical care. It is a gentle book of spring days, best for readers who love rivers, birds, and the Iowa land.
18249-some-summer-days-in-iowa:
Frederick John Lazell wrote Some Summer Days in Iowa, printed in Cedar Rapids in 1909 by the Torch Press. Lazell takes Thoreau's rule that each page of a seasons book should be written in its own season, out of doors, in its own place.

The book opens on an old road in July, where a soft haze hangs over oak leaves, born of grass, trees, and billions of leaf pores. Spores, pollen, and dust of sunshine float in the light, while a farmer's buggy stirs the haze. Lazell writes with a naturalist's wonder. It is a gentle, summer companion to his spring days, full of Iowa light and life.
20961-the-masques-of-ottawa:
No parliament stands midway of so vast a land as Ottawa's, says The Masques of Ottawa. Dominick (Dom) Duffy's sketches name Hull across the river as some folks' fonder choice. Prophets, dreamers, and giants of energy scheme on Parliament Hill in his pages.

Canadian politics takes the stage as a masque of types and turns. Builders of a young nation scheme to draw vast lands into one audience. Duffy writes with a newsman's zest for the Hill's cast and colour. Readers get Ottawa before the First World War, raw, grand, and sure its show had only just begun to draw the nation in.
21389-ronald-morton-or-the-fire-ships-a-:
A castle in Shetland holds the key to a lost claim in W. H. G. Kingston's Ronald Morton, or the Fire Ships. The Morton family may hold rights to a title and lands in Spain. Spanish holders of those lands know the true heir lives in the far north, and their agent is a priest.

Around that puzzle Kingston builds a sea tale set just after the long war with France. Tall ships, fire ships, and Spanish sails fill the pages. The reader must work out, step by step, who Ronald Morton really is. Seamanship and a family mystery carry this long and gripping story together.
22321-john-splendid-the-tale-of-a-poor-g:
Neil Munro wrote John Splendid, the tale of a poor gentleman and a little warrior. The story is set in Scotland less than two hundred years before his time. Munro warns readers how familiar that old world will feel.

Streets, lanes, and tenements in these pages resemble those of his own day. Yet bracken once waved on the promontory where towns now stand. That contrast frames a tale of a gentleman with little money and much honor. Munro was a noted Scottish writer of Highland life. His book offers period adventure told with local knowledge and a storyteller's ease.
25931-science-and-the-infinite-or-throug:
Sydney T. Klein seeks the reality behind the veil of things in this book, first printed in 1912 and reprinted in 1917. Dedicated to Arthur James Balfour, it runs in eight views, from clearing the approach and the vision through mysticism and symbolism, love in action, the physical film, space, time, and creation. Klein holds that mankind still needs symbols to lift abstract thought, as children need picture books.

One striking image shows a magnetized bar that can sway a second bar at a distance, once the second bar has been brought into full sympathy with the first. Klein uses such facts to argue for a hidden unity behind matter and mind. The book is a mystic's tour of science, asking readers to look through a window in a blank wall toward the infinite.
29231-she-would-be-a-soldier-or-the-plai:
Mordecai Manuel Noah wrote this play in three acts, first performed in Philadelphia on June 21, 1819. Noah, born in Philadelphia in 1785 to a family of Portuguese Jewish descent, was apprenticed to a carver and gilder but spent his evenings at the Franklin Library and the theatre. He later met John and Steven Decatur among his schoolfellows.

She Would Be a Soldier, or The Plains of Chippewa, takes its second title from the War of 1812 battle at Chippewa. Its heroine insists on a soldier's life, and the play follows her through camp and battle. Readers get an early American patriotic drama, notable for its woman soldier and for its staging of a recent American victory.
29277-mountain-meditations-and-some-subj:
L. Lind-af-Hageby published this book in London in 1917 with George Allen and Unwin. Lind-af-Hageby, author of a study of August Strindberg, belongs, she writes, to the great and mystic brotherhood of mountain worshippers, a motley crowd from all lands and ages. The sight and smell of mountains affect them like nothing else on earth.

Mountain-Tops opens the book, followed by essays on the borderland, reformers, nationality, and religion in transition. The later subjects of the day and the war bring the mountain view to current questions. Readers get a wartime book of reflection, where climbing becomes a way of thinking about nations, faith, and reform.
31113-company-a-corps-of-engineers-u-s-a:
Gustavus W. Smith, formerly a lieutenant of engineers, wrote this 1896 history of Company A, Corps of Engineers, in the Mexican War of 1846 to 1848. Raised under the act of May 1846, the company trained, waited on the Rio Grande, and marched to Victoria and Tampico. It landed at Vera Cruz and fought its way through Puebla and Churubusco to the capture of Mexico City.

Six chapters carry the unit from enlistment to its return to West Point, with appendices on promotions and on Wilcox's history of the war. Smith writes as a participant officer, so the book pairs official reports with firsthand detail on bridging, siege work, and marching, giving readers a soldier's view of the engineers' war.
31335-history-of-the-constitutions-of-io:
Benjamin F. Shambaugh, professor of political science at the University of Iowa, wrote this history of Iowa's constitutions, published by the Historical Department of Iowa in Des Moines in 1902. It follows the territory and then the state through its successive attempts to frame a fundamental law, including debates over boundaries. One proposal would have set the northern border at the St. Peters River, now the Minnesota River.

The book explains how each constitution took shape, what it settled, and what it left open. For readers of American state history, it shows constitution-making as a practical struggle over land, representation, and powers, not an abstract exercise. Shambaugh's academic treatment keeps the focus on documents, conventions, and the choices that shaped Iowa's government.
3136-the-complete-project-gutenberg-writ:
This omnibus holds Warner's full Project Gutenberg writings in one volume. Baddeck and That Sort of Thing and My Summer in a Garden open the set. Backlog Studies and In the Wilderness follow, with Captain John Smith and The Story of Pocahontas. Saunterings, Being a Boy, and On Horseback sit beside essays like As We Were Saying.

Read straight through, the set shows Warner's whole range. Travel sketches, garden notes, wilderness humor, biography, and social comment share one clear, friendly voice. It works as a one-volume library of a writer who helped shape the American essay, and as a way to follow one mind across a long career.
3287-the-man-from-glengarry-a-tale-of-th:
Ralph Connor dedicates this tale to Glengarry's men, whose patient courage and godly fear helped shape the Canadian West's empire. His preface mourns a vanished world: the solid forests of Glengarry are gone, and with them the men who conquered them. The early days' way of living and kind of character have vanished as well, for good.

The Ottawa lumber country gives the novel its ground: rivers, camps, and the hard work of the shanties. Connor writes of Scottish settlers turned lumbermen, with faith as their anchor. The forest is both workplace and proving ground for the men who felled it, and faith is their anchor.
39346-baltimore-and-the-nineteenth-of-ap:
A study of the Baltimore riot by George William Brown. N Murray published it at Baltimore in 1887 for Johns Hopkins University. Brown had been Baltimore's mayor in 1861. He was later chief judge of its supreme bench. A map shows the railroad route through the city. President Street station to Camden Street station is its deadly stretch.

The first blood shed in the war titles an early section. An assassination plot against the incoming president also features. Brown then argues the constitutional compromises on slavery. The Sixth Massachusetts regiment's fight through Baltimore anchors chapter four. Bridge burning and telegrams to Lincoln follow. Five hundred thousand dollars armed the city's defence. Brown writes as participant and apologist together. His account is a primary source for the war's first week.
39539-the-cambrian-sketch-book-tales-sce:
The Cambrian Sketch-Book, a gathering of tales, scenes, and legends of wild Wales, was written by R Rice Davies. Davies was a Welsh author who also wrote on tax law and local causes. He dedicated the book to Lady Llanover, a known friend and patron of Welsh culture. His letter to her praises her deep knowledge of Welsh history, poetry, and legend.

The preface frames Wales as a land rich in old lore for the antiquary and the general reader alike. The pieces draw on past deeds, dark and splendid, tied to Welsh places. Legends that cling to nearly every corner of the country fill much of the book.
39952-the-iowa:
The Iowa is a reprint of an old monograph on the Ioway people, edited by William Harvey Miner and issued at Cedar Rapids in 1911. The text first ran in The Indian Record, as published by Thomas Foster. Miner adds an introduction and notes through the text. Pictures and a map go with the volume.

The book is dedicated to a lover of books and of men. That man is praised as a student of aboriginal history. The Ioway monograph itself starts the body of the work. Such reprints saved rare pieces on Native peoples from loss. Editors of that age hunted down old papers on the tribes. Miner gives readers the record with aids to its sense. The volume serves students of the peoples of the plains and their past.
463-the-red-badge-of-courage-an-episode-:
Stephen Crane follows a young Union private, Henry Fleming, through his first battle in this Civil War classic. Henry joins with grand dreams of glory, then flees in panic when the fighting turns hot. Shame, a wound won by accident, and a second chance shape his long day under fire.

Crane writes battle as a blur of smoke, noise, and rumor, seen through one boy's mind. The red badge of the title is not a medal but a head wound. The novel endures as a stark study of fear and courage, where a soldier learns that bravery grows less from ideals than from standing with his mates.
46807-lyman-s-history-of-old-walla-walla:
Lyman's History of Old Walla Walla County, volume one, is a county history by Lyman, published in Chicago in 1918 by Clarke. The county of the title embraces Walla Walla, Columbia, Garfield, and Asotin counties in the state of Washington. The work is illustrated, and a portrait of the author heads the volume.

The first part treats the county and its earliest stages. Chapters cover the physical features, soil, climate, and watercourses, then the native races of the region. The first explorers and their routes follow, with the fur trade and its traders. The missionary period and the Indian wars close the first part. The second part turns to settlement: the organisation of the county, the founding of the city, and the times of cowboys, miners, and vigilantes. Political history, the early transport age, and the growth of industry complete the plan.
48836-across-the-reef-the-marine-assault:
Colonel Joseph Alexander, a retired Marine, wrote Across the Reef, the short history of the assault on Tarawa in the Marines in World War II series. The battle for Betio island in November 1943 was the Corps' first great test of landing against a fortified reef.

The contents march by the day. D-Day at Betio falls on November 20, 1943, then D+1 and D+2, and the mopping up to November 28. Sidebars fill the margins: the 2nd Marine Division, General Julian Smith, the Japanese landing forces, and the amphibian tractors. Colonel Shoup, who commanded ashore, gets his own sidebar. The text opens in August 1943, when Admiral Spruance flew in secret to New Zealand to tell Smith to get ready. Veterans and students get the reef and the price, in the Corps' own account.
49119-the-final-campaign-marines-in-the-:
Colonel Joseph Alexander, a Marine officer retired, wrote this short history of the Marines in the victory on Okinawa. It belongs to the Marines in World War II Commemorative Series. Photographs from the Department of Defense run through it, among them the flag raised over Shuri Castle on May 30, 1945.

The chapters count down to Love-Day, the landing, then follow the move to contact and the air and sea battles. The assault on Shuri takes the center, with sidebars on Marine artillery, tanks, and air support. A photo shows two Marines advancing on Wana Ridge on May 18, 1945. The book closes the loop of the island fight and ends with a legacy section. Veterans and students get the last great campaign of the Pacific war in brief, clear form.
60372-the-white-chief-of-the-ottawa:
The White Chief of the Ottawa, by Bertha Wright Carr Harris, was printed at Toronto in 1903, with seven full page plates by John Innes. Carr Harris states in her preface that the book is not fiction. It tells the life of Philemon Wright and his kin.

Wright and his family were the first settlers in the Ottawa district. Carr Harris drew on Wright diary and letters from 1806 to 1816, and on old travel books and tales of first settlers. She grants that the love tales of Abbie and Chrissy rest on fact in a looser way. Chapter heads name voyageurs, an Indian suitor, and convent days. Readers get a warm family tale that keeps close to the true past of a new town.
63118-historic-homes-fort-dodge-iowa:
Historic Homes of Fort Dodge, Iowa is a photo and text survey from 1975. The Blanden Federation of Arts put the book out in April that year. Allen Loomis took the photographs and Karl Haugen wrote the text. Messenger Printing of Fort Dodge set and printed the whole work. An index of homes sits at the back, with a map before it.

The Oleson home on Third Avenue South opens the long house list. Oleson, a pioneer druggist and giver, built the brick house in 1906. Green tile roofs it, and a pipe organ stood inside for years. Three floors hold five bedrooms, two baths, and a recreation room. The organ later went to the nurses' home of Lutheran Hospital. Oleson came from Norway and built his drug firm in town. His 1894 drug store block stood at Central Avenue and Eighth Street.
66063-the-open-polar-sea-a-narrative-of-:
The Open Polar Sea is a narrative of a voyage toward the North Pole by Doctor I I Hayes. The voyage was made in the schooner United States, and the book was published in New York in eighteen sixty seven. A portrait of Hayes fronts the volume. He dedicates it to a Philadelphia friend who backed the venture.

Hayes tells the story of discovery in Arctic waters in the first person. Ice, cold, and the search for open water beyond the ice are the heart of such a voyage. The title states the theory that drove it, that an open sea lay near the Pole. The book is both a travel record and a case for that lost idea.
70028-a-catalogue-of-remarkable-books-pu:
A Catalogue of Remarkable Books, published by George Redway in eighteen eighty seven, lists his firm's stock. Redway kept his shop at York Street, Covent Garden, in London that year. The motto on the title page is the Latin phrase Tolle, Lege. Its first and longest entry sells the Kabbala Unveiled in one handsome volume.

That work holds three books of the Zohar in English dress for the reader. MacGregor Mathers turned them from a Latin version and checked the Hebrew text. Long quotes praise the Kabbalah as a secret lore handed down from angels. Ginsburg is quoted calling it a theosophy that gripped great minds for centuries. Lully, Reuchlin, Pico, Agrippa, Fludd, and More are named among its captives. The rest of the catalogue lists more works of the same occult bent.
73-the-red-badge-of-courage-an-episode-o:
A young Union soldier longs for a wound that will prove his courage. Stephen Crane's Red Badge of Courage follows Henry Fleming through his first battle in the Civil War. Rumors, camp talk, and the sight of enemy fires open the novel.

Henry flees his first fight, then returns to the line and fights hard. Crane tracks fear, shame, and pride inside one mind rather than grand strategy. The battle scenes stay close to mud, noise, and smoke. The short novel became a classic of war fiction. Crane, who never saw battle, wrote a war novel praised for its inward truth about fear.
74401-elkswatawa:
An unnamed author wrote Elkswatawa, or The Prophet of the West, a tale of the frontier published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1836. The book appeared in two volumes; this file holds volume one. The dedication explains its aim. The author enlarged on a portion of national history, setting out the lives of two celebrated Native leaders in connected form. Lines from Bryant stand at the front.

The preface tells how the tale began. The author lived for some time in the western part of the Union. He visited many tribes along the frontier and watched their customs closely. Elkswatawa was the Shawnee prophet, brother of Tecumseh, whose religious movement and its clash with American expansion shaped the old Northwest. The novel turns that history into a frontier tale for the readers of 1836, close to the events it describes.
74874-siwa:
Siwa, the Oasis of Jupiter Ammon, by C Dalrymple Belgrave, was first published in 1923 in London. Sketches and photographs by the author fill the book. General Sir Reginald Wingate writes the opening words. A first view shows the walls of Siwa, a walled town in the desert west of Egypt.

Early chapters cross the coast belt and then the desert, by camel, from Sollum to Siwa. They note Arab tents, meals, hounds, and hunting on the way. A long history part treats the temple of Ammon, a lost army of Cambyses, and the visit of Alexander. Later parts treat Arab, Turkish, and war years. Travel readers get a full account of a famed oracle town.
britannica-1911-batwa:
Batwa is the name of a tribe of African pygmies in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They live in the hilly country round Wissmann Falls in the Kasai district of the Belgian Congo. They were found in 1880 by Pogge and Wissmann, and are held true members of the negrito family south of the Congo. They are well made, seldom over four feet high, with a yellow-brown skin far lighter than that of their Bantu neighbours.

Hunting is the Batwa's whole life. They are wanderers who plant nothing and keep no beasts but a small hunting dog. Their weapon is a tiny bow with arrows that are most often poisoned. They run through the jungle “like grasshoppers” and attack even elephants and buffalo. Palm-wine, traded to the Baluba for grain, is their only other work. They are noted as keeping one wife and showing strong love within the family.
britannica-1911-biwa:
Biwa is a lake in the province of Omi, Japan. It measures 36 miles long by 12 miles at its widest breadth. Its area is 180 square miles, and it lies about 330 feet above sea level. Its greatest depth is some 300 feet. A few small islands sit in the lake, the chief being Chikubu-shima at the northern end. Tradition says Biwa and Mount Fuji rose together in an earthquake of 286 BC.

Mountains slope to the water on the west shore, while a wide plain opens east. A river drains the lake from its southern end toward Osaka bay. That river takes the names Seta, Uji, and Yodo along its course. The lake abounds with fish, and its scenery is called remarkable. The 1911 Britannica entry lists the famous eight landscapes of Omi around its shores. A canal of 1890 links the lake with Kyoto by water.
britannica-1911-burlington-iowa:
Burlington, a city on the Mississippi river in Iowa, is described in a full place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of Des Moines county in the south east of the state. About twenty four thousand people lived there at the later count in the entry. Three rail lines serve the city, and river trade is large.

Many homes stand on bluffs with fine views of the river. Stone from local quarries serves as building stock. Crapo Park, a hundred acres along the river, is a chief draw. Key buildings include the court house, the free library, and the post office. Factories made lumber, pearl buttons, rail cars, engines, and flour, among much else. The entry traces the town from a fur post to an early seat of two territorial law bodies.
britannica-1911-chilwa:
Chilwa, incorrectly called Shirwa, is a shallow lake in south-east Africa, south-south-east of Lake Nyasa, lying between 15 and 15 degrees 35 minutes south. The lake is drying up, and in dry seasons such as 1879 and 1903 its open water shrinks to a number of large pools. It once seems to have drained northward to the Lujenda branch of the Rovuma. A wooded ridge now divides it from that river.

That ridge stands some 30 to 40 feet above the surrounding plains, a small height with a large effect on the lake. Four islands lie in the water, the largest rising 500 feet above it. David Livingstone discovered the lake in 1859, the entry says, and called it Shirwa from a mishearing of the native name. Drying, a lost outlet and Livingstone's error together make the substance of this notice.
britannica-1911-malwa:
Malwa, a historic province of India, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In the strict sense the name fits a hilly table-land bounded south by the Vindhyan range. Its waters drain north into the river Chambal. In wider use it also takes in the Nerbudda valley to the south.

The name is traced to the old Malava tribe, who founded an era dated from fifty-seven years before Christ. The Paramara clan, famed Rajputs, ruled the land for some four centuries from Ujjain and then Dhar. Muslim armies invaded in 1235, and an independent kingdom arose in 1401. Its greatest king, Hoshang Shah, made Mandu his capital and graced it with grand buildings. Akbar annexed Malwa to the Mogul empire in 1562, and the Marathas seized it as that empire broke apart.
britannica-1911-mount-vernon-iowa:
Mount Vernon is a town of Linn County, Iowa. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica centers it on its college. It stands east of Cedar Rapids on a rail line. Its count slipped from about sixteen hundred in 1900 to fewer in 1910.

Cornell College gives the small town its whole weight. The school is Methodist and teaches men and women together. It opened as a conference seminary in 1853. A charter of 1857 gave it the name it still bears. That name honors a New York iron maker who aided it. The college holds a music school, an art school, and more. Forty teachers served about seven hundred fifty students in 1908. The town was settled in 1842 and laid out in 1847. Town incorporation came in 1869, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-nassarawa:
Nassarawa is a province article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Nassarawa was a province of the British protectorate of northern Nigeria. It lies on the northern bank of the River Benue. That winding river forms the province's southern frontier.

The entry sets out the province's neighbours on every side. Muri lay to the east, Bauchi to the north-east, and Zaria to the north. Nupe and Kabba closed the west. Its area came to 18,000 square miles, with an estimated 1,500,000 people. Mountainous country crosses parts of the province. It holds valuable forests and many fertile river valleys. Native products named include rubber, palm kernels, and beni seed. Cotton was grown extensively across the province. The piece gives colonial readers the size, bounds, and wealth of a West African territory.
britannica-1911-oshawa: Oshawa is a short town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Ontario in Canada. It stands on Lake Ontario by a rail line. It lies east north east of Toronto city. Its count in 1901 was just under four thousand souls. It serves as a port of entry for the state. Mills there grind flour and wool and grain. Works make pianos, farm tools, and carriages as well. Foundries, tanneries, and canning works give more jobs. A college for women and good schools serve the town.
britannica-1911-peshwa:
Peshwa was the title of the head of the Mahratta confederacy in India, explained in a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is Persian for leader or guide. At first the peshwa was no more than a prime minister to his prince. In time he pushed his master aside and took the rule of the state.

The post then passed from father to son as a family right, with its seat at Poona. The last peshwa, Baji Rao, fell out with the British and was cast from his throne in 1818. His adopted son, Nana Sahib, played a chief part in the Mutiny of 1857. The entry says he acted to win back rights he held to be his own, taken from him by the British.
britannica-1911-rewa:
Rewa is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rewa, also spelled Riwa, is a native state of Central India in the Bagelkhand agency. It is the only large state in Bagelkhand and the second largest in Central India, with an area of about thirteen thousand square miles. The state falls into two clear parts. The north is a plateau between the Kaimur hills and the Vindhyas, farmed and well peopled.

Water is plentiful, and the land is full of large tanks. Yet these are not used for watering fields. The chief rivers are the Sone and the Tons, and neither can take boats. The count of 1901 found more than one million three hundred thousand people. More than a third of the state is forest, yielding timber and lac.
britannica-1911-sadowa: Sadowa is a village of Bohemia, in Austria, four miles north-west of Koniggratz. It had 183 people in 1900, all of them Czech. Sadowa, with the small wood that stands next to it, was one of the chief posts of the Prussians in a great battle. That clash was among the most hotly fought of the fight now as a rule called by the name of Koniggratz. The battle is treated in the article on the Seven Weeks' War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iowa:
Iowa, midway between the Atlantic and the Pacific and wedged between the Mississippi and the Missouri, receives a full state portrait here. It runs 310 miles east to west and 210 miles north to south. It covers 56,025 square miles, about the size of Wisconsin or Illinois. The Mississippi bounds it east. The Missouri and Big Sioux bound it west. Its surface is rolling prairie, part of the Great Central Plain.

From that geography the entry moves through resources, people, schools, government, and history. It then gives extended room to Catholic life. Missions, parishes, and the dioceses that grew with settlement fill that room. Readers get a state survey in the encyclopedia's standard shape, useful for the facts of a place and for the story of its church at the turn of the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ottawa:
Ottawa is a Canadian archdiocese that once covered the whole Ottawa Valley, before Pontiac, Pembroke, and Temiskamingue were cut from it. It still spans 10,000 square miles in Ontario counties Carleton, Russell, Prescott, and Lanark, and Quebec counties Wright, Labelle, Argenteuil, Terrebonne, and Montcalm. The 1901 census counted 158,000 Catholics there, 128,000 French-speaking and 30,000 English-speaking.

Ottawa city rose in 1827 with works on the Rideau Canal, first named Bytown for Colonel By, the engineer in charge. Water power and a site at the Chaudiere Falls made it an industrial centre. Rome raised it to a see in 1848, and it took the name Ottawa on incorporation in 1854. The entry closes with its archbishops, its Catholic university, its schools, hospitals, and homes for emigrant children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Ottawa's university is conducted by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate and was founded in 1848. It was incorporated in 1849 as the College of Bytown, taking the original name of the city chosen in 1866 as capital of the Canadian Dominion, now Ottawa. The title changed in 1861 to the College of Ottawa, and civil charter in 1866 conferred the power to grant degrees. The university thus began its full secular existence with the confederation of the Canadian provinces.

A brief from Leo XIII dated 5 February 1889 lifted the college and Ottawa's State University to Catholic university rank. The brief willed that the Archbishop of Ottawa serve as apostolic chancellor. The entry follows the institution's growth with the Dominion, its faculties, and its bilingual teaching, a compact history of higher learning in Canada's capital.
clerambault-the-story-of-an-independent-:
Clerambault: The Story of an Independent Spirit During the War, by Romain Rolland, follows one man's conscience against the herd spirit of wartime. Rolland's preface grants that he lent his hero some ideas. The man's character, life, and inward labyrinth, he insists, are the hero's own: weak, timid, and sincere.

An introduction first printed in Swiss newspapers in December 1917 states the theme. The book is not about the war, though the war's shadow lies over it. Its subject is the individual soul swallowed by the soul of the multitude. Clerambault, an ordinary man who depends on the love and approval of others, must decide whether he is strong enough to speak and bear their hatred.
doe-osti-2574272-cactus-co-sub-2-sub-aer:
SRI International final report DE-AR0001583, led by Gabriel Iftime and covering July 2022 to June 2025, reports the CACTUS project under ARPA-E. The aim was direct air capture of carbon dioxide using aerogel sorbents, feather-light porous solids with huge internal surface. A partner team at Arizona State University ran many of the sorption measurements while SRI's own setup was repaired.

Progress was uneven, and the report says so. The best early sorbent took up only 0.03 millimoles of carbon dioxide per gram, far too little. A much stronger material, above 0.44 millimoles per gram, arrived late in the project. It could not be tested across the full humidity range before time ran out. Milestones along the way included gram-scale aerogel batches, water and carbon dioxide isotherms from dry to saturated air, and reviews of sorbent and air contactor designs.
doe-osti-2584416-strontium-speciation-in:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory study by Amanda R. Bubas, Elise R. Conte, Richard M. Cox, Tatiana G. Levitskaia, and colleagues asks what strontium actually looks like inside tank waste. Strontium's chemistry in Hanford's tanks decides how it behaves during treatment, yet in those brines it never travels alone; it complexes with whatever anions surround it. The team used electrospray ionization mass spectrometry, with tandem MS and infrared dissociation methods, to name the complexes directly.

Experiments started with strontium nitrate, then staged competitions. Nitrite, hydroxide, and chloride each challenged nitrate for the metal, alone and all together, mapping which ligands win under which conditions. Speciation sounds academic until a separation process fails because the target ion was wearing an unexpected partner. For waste treatment design, knowing strontium's molecular company is the difference between a process modeled on the real chemistry and one modeled on a guess.
doe-osti-2589920-strong-grid-resiliency-:
San Diego Gas and Electric's final technical report on award EE0009027 covers a full-renewable microgrid at Borrego Springs, California, upgraded with help from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Lead authors Laurence Abcede, Kimberly McGrath, and Jose Cardenas report for the utility, with Annabelle Pratt and co-authors for the laboratory. A battery inverter was given grid-forming controls so it can lead the island grid on its own.

Laboratory hardware-in-the-loop tests rehearsed the risky moves before field trials. A power interface with an inductor let the real inverter switch between following the grid and forming it during simulated islanding. Tests covered planned islanding, black start from dead, and load steps while islanded, checking voltage and frequency control. Field rules in the report cap the power flow at plus or minus 50 kilowatts before the controller allows islanding.
doe-osti-3002278-advanced-data-managemen:
Naushita Sharma, Paul Lemar, Christopher Price, and Rima Asmar Awad cover the data side of wastewater work in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4027, dated October 2025. Treatment plants now stream sensor data on flow, oxygen demand, and chemical load. Advanced data management turns that stream into decisions: when to aerate, dose, or hold flow during storms.

The report surveys current practice and tools, including smart wet-weather control systems documented by the Environmental Protection Agency. Artificial intelligence applications in treatment get a review of their own. Cybersecurity earns a place too, through the NIST framework, since networked controls widen the attack surface. Plant operators and utility IT staff are the readers. The message is that data systems now sit beside pumps and basins as core plant infrastructure.
doe-osti-3004690-reduction-of-porosity-i:
Eric R. McCaslin, Alex D. Cozzi, and Katie A. Hill test a waste form improvement in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2024-00633, Revision 0, dated October 2025. Saltstone, a cement-like grout, locks low-activity salt waste into solid blocks at the Savannah River Site. Some contaminants, including methyl mercury, iodine-129, technetium-99, and nitrate, are not perfectly held by the current recipe.

The idea under test is simple: less pore space should mean slower escape for everything at once. The team lowered the water-to-binder ratio of the standard saltstone mix and cast test cylinders. Porosity fell as predicted, and leaching resistance improved with it. The trade-offs of a drier mix for plant-scale pouring bound the practical use. Results support porosity reduction as one lever for widening where grout waste forms can serve.
doe-osti-3011001-slow-strain-rate-testin:
Slow strain rate testing of A537 tank wall steel under Savannah River Site waste simulants is reported by Rasmussen, Wiersma, and Neveau in SRNL-STI-2025-00337. The tests probe stress corrosion cracking in dissolved salt solutions, which the work confirms are potent cracking contributors. Round tensile bars were machined to ASTM E8 and tested under ASTM G129.

Findings point to a critical cracking potential tied to passive film behaviour and the nitrite to nitrate ratio. The report recommends added testing to define that potential, long term open circuit measurements, and polarisation studies across simulant chemistries. It also suggests fitting a reference electrode in an actual tank to measure its true potential.
doe-osti-3365143-lanl-institutional-comp:
A Los Alamos National Laboratory Institutional Computing report by Adrian K. Turner, LA-UR-26-24111 and dated May 14, 2026, describes progress toward a digital twin of Arctic sea ice. The twin pairs a high-resolution model with observations so forecasters can predict ice conditions weeks ahead and policymakers can plan for a changing Arctic. The model, DEMSI, represents ice as discrete elements pressing and grinding against each other.

Three advances anchor the year. An ensemble Kalman filter data assimilation system now builds realistic starting conditions from patchy observations. A new coupling method rotates ocean-ice velocities with the Coriolis effect during sub-cycling, improving stability and stress transfer in tests with the DOE ocean model. Deformation analysis also improved. The tools feed toward the DOE's E3SM Earth system model.
doe-osti-3453389-small-modular-reactor-a:
Sandia report SAND2026-25006R, by Alan Evans and Matt McCullough, gives physical protection advice for placing a small modular reactor beside a large light water reactor. The report is dated April 2025 in the text. Shared sites raise new guard and layout questions.

Two layouts are weighed: the small reactor inside the current protected area, or outside it. Scenario walk-throughs test how attackers might reach key buildings. Response force placement shapes those outcomes in the cases shown. Site owners get concrete layout guidance before design locks in. Protection planning stays cheaper when done before concrete is poured.
doe-osti-3740143-workbench-analysis-sequ:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4728, dated July 2026, describes release 4.4 of the WASP software framework. Robert Lefebvre, Brandon Langley, Jordan Lefebvre, and Shane Henderson are the printed authors. Science codes lean on structured text files for settings, models, and data swaps. Each code tends to invent its own dialect, so the same checks get rebuilt again and again. WASP instead parses any supported dialect into one shared tree that keeps values, labels, links, and source spots.

Three services work on the shared tree. One checks files against meaning rules, one pulls out chosen parts on request, and one renders files for display or reuse. Language help, Python hooks, plotting, and command-line tools build on the same base. Since syntax and meaning stay split, a new dialect needs only a fresh reader, not fresh services. The memo replaces a 2017 account of the early design.
doe-osti-3904548-real-time-exoplanet-dir:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2024719, dated September 2026, closes a project on sharper exoplanet imaging. Benjamin Gerard is the printed principal investigator, under project code 24-LW-002. Today's best adaptive optics would fall about a hundredfold short on the giant telescopes now planned. The REDWOODS instrument at Lick Observatory was built to close that gap. It tests second-stage wavefront sensing, the fine correction layer that decides whether a faint planet shows beside its star.

All three headline technologies were validated on the sky. A fast self-coherent camera sensor gained a broadband corrector mode. A fully reflective pyramid sensor mode kept sensitivity across a broad spectrum. New software fused readings from several sensors into one control loop. The title points ahead to a hybrid sensor and science camera for extreme imaging at Keck Observatory. Two 2025 conference papers carry the detailed results.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAWarrenCommis:
On March 12, 1964, Richard Helms of the CIA met J. Lee Rankin, chief counsel of the Warren Commission, with a Mr. Murphy in attendance. This memorandum, released through the CIA's Historical Review Program, records that meeting between the agency and the commission.

The subjects were the heart of the case: Oswald's stay in the Soviet Union and the commission's Oswald memorandum. What the CIA told the commission, and what it held back, became central questions for every later inquiry. The memo is the agency's own note of the encounter, preserved as a primary record of the relationship between the two bodies.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EpsteinEdwardJa: nsia-EpsteinEdwardJayLegend Epstein Edward Jay Legend: the made public government document on Edward Jay Epstein, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers.
legal-status-of-women-in-iowa:
Jennie L. Wilson compiled the Legal Status of Women in Iowa in 1894. Wilson held a law degree and belonged to the Polk County Bar. The Iowa Printing Company issued her book at Des Moines.

Her preface states the aim in direct terms. She presents, briefly, the laws women most need to know. Demand for certain, accurate information was growing, she says. Property, marriage, and rights at law fill the summaries. The book served Iowa women seeking their standing in plain language. Wilson wrote as a woman lawyer for women readers. That pairing was still rare enough to matter in 1894.
little-sky-high-or-the-surprising-doings:
Hezekiah Butterworth wrote this children's tale of Washee-Washee-Wang. The Kentuckiana Digital Library supplied its page images. Butterworth had written In the Days of Jefferson and schoolhouse tales. The book belongs to a Nine to Twelve series for young readers.

Companion volumes in the series include Little Dick's Son. Marcia and the Major and The Children of the Valley appear too. Surprising doings, the title promises, drive its hero's adventures. The story aims its wonders squarely at boys and girls. Harriet Prescott Spofford and Kate Upson Clark wrote companion volumes. The series aimed its stories at readers aged nine to twelve.
native-life-in-south-africa-before-and-s: Native Life in South Africa, Before and Since the European War and the Boer Rebellion is a book by Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the book itself. The title alone frames the subject: the lives of native South Africans, set against two wars named in the title. No year for the book is given in the sample or the record. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
podcast-joerogan-MtoPEub7XwA: Bob Gymlan joins Joe Rogan for episode 2185 of the Joe Rogan Experience. The record kept with the file gives the guest name and the episode number but no topic line, no guest background, and no summary of the talk. The file holds the full transcript of that sitting in the show's long, free form. Listeners will learn the ground covered only from the talk itself, since the record states nothing more than who sat down and which episode it was.
podcast-tuckercarlson-V4hoNaxVSwA:
Radio host Jesse Kelly and former congressional candidate Nicole Shanahan join Tucker Carlson for a three-way conversation. They discuss transhumanism. They also discuss what they call Kamala Harris's plan to take Americans' guns, and how to save Texas. All three treat Texas as the country's last redoubt.

Kelly brings the combat veteran's bluntness. Shanahan brings the convert's zeal from her years in Democratic donor politics. Carlson brings the frame. It joins technology, disarmament, and regional secession of the spirit into one warning. The episode is a panel of allies rather than an interview, and its energy is strategic: how the right should use Texas as its model and fortress. Preserved here is movement talk at full strength, three prominent voices planning aloud for an audience that takes the stakes as stated.
some-spring-days-in-iowa:
Frederick John Lazell wrote Some Spring Days in Iowa. The Torch Press printed it at Cedar Rapids in 1908. A note from Joseph Newton stands at the front. Newton dated it December 1, 1908. The pages shown open at part IV. Its head reads April — Buds and Bird Songs. Lines above it ask if nature has not shown us all. They run from clear space to new buds unfolding.

A strong southeast wind opens Lazell's April. It blows straight up the broad river. It drives big waves against the current. The current pushes at the base of each wave. Their crests fall forward and break into spray. The whole face of the river flecks with whitecaps. Lazell calls that a rare sight on an inland stream.
some-summer-days-in-iowa:
Frederick John Lazell wrote Some Summer Days in Iowa. The Torch Press printed it at Cedar Rapids in 1909. A line from Thoreau heads the book. A book of the seasons, it says, should be written in its own season. It should be written out of doors as well. The pages shown open at part VII. Its head reads An Old Road in July.

A soft haze hangs on the old woods road. It shows only where its tints meet dark oak leaves. Lazell traces the haze to cord grasses by the road. Trees, shrubs, and vines feed it too. Acres of leaves breathe damp into the sun. A second stream of life floats in it. Spores rise from mushrooms past the fence. Pollen lifts from red top grasses. Fine dust hangs in the sunshine itself.
some-winter-days-in-iowa:
Frederick John Lazell wrote Some Winter Days in Iowa. The Torch Press printed it at Cedar Rapids in 1907. A front note by Thomas H. Macbride stands in the book. Macbride dated it October 17, 1907, at Iowa City. Part I bears the head The Woodlands in January. It opens with a broad claim. Man has always turned to nature for relief. Toil and strife drive that turn, Lazell says.

Lazell sees glad signs in the new longing. Folk wish to leave the roar of the streets. They tire of prim town gardens as well. Rich men sell grand city houses for country homes. There they can watch sunrise and the death of day. Cities buy large parks, he notes. States set aside wild tracts for the folk. Tired nerves mend in such places, he holds.
the-complete-project-gutenberg-writings-: Charles D. Warner's entire Project Gutenberg writings are gathered here by David Widger, but only a contents list is present. The list mixes travel and outdoor books. Baddeck and That Sort of Thing stands there, with My Summer in a Garden, Backlog Studies, and In the Wilderness. Tales like How I Killed a Bear and A Fight with a Trout sit beside them. It also folds in the essay volume As We Were Saying and a life of Captain John Smith with the story of Pocahontas. No text follows.
the-man-from-glengarry-a-tale-of-the-ott:
Ralph Connor's The Man from Glengarry, a tale of the Ottawa, is dedicated to the men of Glengarry, builders of the empire of the Canadian West. His preface mourns a vanished world: the solid forests of Glengarry are gone, and with them the men who conquered them and their manner of life. Part of the book's purpose, he says, is to picture those men and their times so they do not drop out of mind.

Connor describes their marks: fierce passions, courage, and loyalty from their blood; patience, resourcefulness, and self-reliance from the forest. Deepest of all was their faith, a religion perhaps narrow but the biggest thing in them. Their sons, he notes, are now found in the Canada beyond the Lakes, where empire is being made and such men are needed.
the-red-badge-of-courage-an-episode-of-t:
Stephen Crane subtitled his Civil War novel an episode of that conflict. He divided it into twenty-four chapters. The opening shows cold lifting reluctantly from the earth. Fog reveals an army resting on the hills. The army wakes to rumors of movement. A river runs amber at its feet. Hostile camp-fires gleam red across it at night.

That famous first page treats the army as one creature. It trembles with eagerness. It watches roads dry from mud into thoroughfares. A contents list of numbered chapters precedes the prose here. Another record in the set carries the same opening. That record has no contents list before it. Readers should expect the same novel in both records.
